title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
description: Brute force to optimized: generating and sorting every number as a string versus navigating a 10-ary lexicographical tree using directly computed subtree sizes.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integers n and k, return the kth smallest integer in the range [1, n] when all the integers are arranged in lexicographical (dictionary/string) order rather than numeric order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, k"],["Output","The kth number in [1, n], ordered lexicographically"],["Goal","Find this without generating and sorting all n numbers"],["Constraints","1 <= k <= n <= 10^9"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Lexicographical order naturally forms a tree: 1 is followed by 10, 11, ..., 19, then 100, ...","Think of the numbers as nodes in a 10-ary tree (children formed by appending a digit)"],["n and k can be up to a billion","Count how many numbers lie within a subtree directly, to skip entire subtrees without visiting each number"]]}

blocks.text: Sort the numbers 1 through n as if they were strings (so 10 comes right after 1, before 2), and return the number sitting at the kth position in that order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Navigating a Dictionary-Ordered Filing Tree
blocks.text: Picture every number as a folder, where folder 1 contains subfolders 10, 11, ..., 19, and folder 10 contains 100, 101, and so on, exactly like a phone directory or dictionary. Walking through this tree in a specific depth-first order visits numbers in exact lexicographical order.

blocks.caption: Lexicographical order forms a 10-ary tree; counting a subtree's size lets you skip past it

blocks.text: In lexicographical order, the numbers 1 through 13 read: 1, 10, 11, 12, 13, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The 2nd number in that order is 10.
With only the number 1 available, the 1st (and only) number is 1.

Before generating and sorting all n numbers as strings, notice that lexicographical order corresponds exactly to a depth-first walk of a 10-ary tree, where a number's "subtree" is counted directly with arithmetic.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In lexicographical order, a number is immediately followed by its "children," formed by appending each digit 0 through 9 (as long as the result stays at most n).

Observation 2: The number of nodes in the subtree rooted at a given prefix can be counted directly, level by level, by counting how many numbers with that prefix exist at each digit length, without listing them.

Observation 3: Starting at 1 and tracking how many steps (numbers visited) remain to reach the kth one, if a prefix's entire subtree size is smaller than the remaining steps, the whole subtree can be skipped at once by moving to the next sibling prefix; otherwise, descend into the first child.

Observation 4: Repeating this skip-or-descend decision converges on the exact kth number, having only ever counted subtree sizes, never listed individual numbers.

This leads to walking the 10-ary lexicographical tree starting from 1, counting each candidate subtree's size directly, and either skipping past it (moving to the next sibling) or descending into it, until exactly k minus 1 steps have been taken.
Generate every number from 1 to n, convert each to a string, sort them lexicographically, and pick the kth one.

items: Generate the list of numbers from 1 to n.
Convert each to a string and sort the list of strings.
Return the number at position k minus 1 in that sorted order.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: generate, stringify, and sort every number, then index in

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every number from 1 to n is materialized as a string before sorting.
With n up to a billion, both generating and sorting this many strings is completely impractical.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), generating and sorting n strings.
Space: O(n), storing every number as a string.

Limitation: with n and k both up to a billion, materializing and sorting every number is far too slow and memory-heavy; a way to count and skip entire groups of numbers without listing them is required.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating every number is unnecessary: lexicographical order has a predictable tree structure, and the SIZE of any prefix's subtree (how many numbers from 1 to n start with that prefix) can be computed directly with arithmetic.

How to count a subtree's size: starting from the prefix itself, at each digit length, count how many numbers with that prefix (and one more digit, two more digits, and so on) fall within [1, n], summing across all lengths until the range no longer overlaps [1, n].

How to use that count to navigate: starting at 1 with k minus 1 steps remaining, if the current prefix's subtree size is at most the remaining steps, skip the whole subtree (move to the next sibling, and subtract the subtree size from the remaining steps); otherwise, descend into the first child (append a 0) and use up exactly one step.

The core idea: walk the lexicographical tree from 1, using subtree-size counts to skip or descend, converging on the kth number without ever listing individual numbers.

Start at curr equal to 1, with k decremented by 1 (since curr itself counts as the first step). While steps remain, count the subtree size rooted at curr (how many numbers from curr's prefix range fall within [1, n]). If that size is at most the remaining k, move to the next sibling (curr plus 1) and subtract the subtree size from k. Otherwise, descend into the first child (curr times 10) and subtract 1 from k. Return curr once k reaches 0.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: count subtree sizes directly, skip or descend, converge on the kth number

blocks.text: Counting how many numbers with a given prefix fall within [1, n], level by level, correctly computes the size of that prefix's entire subtree in lexicographical order. Comparing that size to the remaining step count determines whether the whole subtree can be skipped in one jump (moving to the next sibling and reducing k by the whole subtree size) or must be entered (moving to the first child and reducing k by exactly 1), converging on the kth number after using up exactly k minus 1 total steps.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((log n) squared), since each subtree-size count takes O(log n), and the number of skip/descend steps is also O(log n).
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This problem treats lexicographical order as a 10-ary tree traversal, where counting a subtree's size directly, rather than listing its contents, allows entire branches to be skipped in a single step, converging on the kth number in a handful of arithmetic operations.

items: Forgetting to bound the subtree size counting by n plus 1, which would overcount numbers beyond the allowed range.
Mixing up when to subtract the whole subtree size (skipping) versus subtracting just 1 (descending).
Off-by-one errors in the initial k minus 1 adjustment, since curr equal to 1 is itself the first visited number.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k = 1","The answer is always 1, the lexicographically smallest number."],["k = n","The answer is the lexicographically largest number, often ending in the highest possible trailing digits."]]}

blocks.text: Framing the problem explicitly as a 10-ary tree traversal, where subtree sizes are computed directly instead of listed, is the key insight that turns an O(n log n) brute force into a near-instant arithmetic walk.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "n and k can be up to a billion, how do you avoid generating every number", think: count subtree sizes directly in the lexicographical tree, and skip or descend accordingly.

items: How would you find the RANK of a given number, instead of finding the number at a given rank?
How does this subtree-counting technique generalize to other lexicographically-ordered structures, like strings over a different alphabet?
Any "navigate a tree using subtree-size counts, skip or descend" problem, a broader technique beyond just numeric ordering.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. The optimized subtree-counting approach runs in O((log n) squared) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: treating lexicographical order as a 10-ary tree, navigated using directly computed subtree sizes.
Core Idea: count how many numbers fall within a prefix's subtree directly; skip the whole subtree if it is smaller than the remaining steps, otherwise descend into it, converging on the kth number.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O((log n) squared) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a prefix's subtree size in lexicographical order is directly computable, letting entire subtrees be skipped without ever listing their contents.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known hard problem; correctly counting subtree sizes and navigating skip-versus-descend decisions are the trickiest details.
One line memory trick: lexicographical order is a 10-ary tree; count subtree sizes to skip or descend.
